note: Closing quotation mark added; source leaves this speech paragraph unclosed.
replacement: “Our constitution does not copy the laws of our neighbors. We are a pattern to others rather than imitators of them. Our administration favors the many instead of the few, and that is why it is called a democracy. In private disputes the laws give equal justice to all. As for social standing, advancement in public life goes to reputation for capacity, and class considerations are not allowed to interfere with merit. Nor does poverty bar the way: a man who can serve the state is not hindered by the obscurity of his condition. The freedom we enjoy in public life extends also to our ordinary life. In that, far from keeping a jealous watch on one another, we do not feel called upon to be angry with a neighbor for doing as he likes, or even to give him those injurious looks which cannot fail to give offense, though they inflict no actual penalty. But this ease in our private relations does not make us lawless as citizens. Fear is our chief safeguard against that. It teaches us to obey the magistrates and the laws, above all those that protect the injured, whether they are actually on the statute book or belong to the unwritten code that cannot be broken without acknowledged disgrace.

note: Closing quotation mark added; source leaves this speech paragraph unclosed.
replacement: “We also provide plenty of ways for the mind to refresh itself after business. We celebrate games and sacrifices all the year round, and the elegance of our private establishments gives daily pleasure and helps to banish gloom. And because our city is so large, the produce of the whole world is drawn into our harbor, so that the Athenian enjoys the fruits of other countries as familiarly as those of his own.

note: Closing quotation mark added; source leaves this speech paragraph unclosed. Also wealth is for use, not action, and the purpose clause (in order to keep the recipient in debt) was lost.
replacement: “These are not the only points in which our city deserves admiration. We cultivate refinement without extravagance and knowledge without softness. We employ wealth more for use than for show, and we think the real disgrace of poverty lies not in admitting to it but in not struggling against it. Our public men also have private affairs to attend to, and our ordinary citizens, though busy with their trades, are still fair judges of public matters. We are unlike any other nation in this: we regard a man who takes no part in these duties as useless, not as unambitious. We Athenians can at all events judge a proposal, even if we cannot originate one; and we do not see discussion as a stumbling-block in the way of action. We think it an indispensable preliminary to any wise action at all. In our enterprises, again, we present the singular spectacle of daring and deliberation, each carried to its highest point and both united in the same persons, although decision is usually the fruit of ignorance, and hesitation of reflection. But the palm of courage will surely be awarded most justly to those who know best the difference between hardship and pleasure and yet are never tempted to shrink from danger. In generosity, too, we are singular, since we win our friends by conferring favors, not by receiving them. Yet of course the giver of a favor is the firmer friend of the two, wishing by continued kindness to keep the recipient in his debt. The debtor feels less keenly, because he knows that his return will be a payment, not a free gift. And only the Athenians, fearless of consequences, confer their benefits not out of calculations of expediency but in the confidence of liberality.

note: Closing quotation mark added; source leaves this speech paragraph unclosed.
replacement: “If I have dwelt at some length on the character of our country, it was to show that we have more at stake in this struggle than men who have no such blessings to lose, and at the same time to establish by definite proofs the panegyric of the men over whom I am now speaking. That panegyric is now largely complete. The Athens I have celebrated is only what the heroism of these men and their like has made her; and their fame, unlike that of most Hellenes, will be found to match their deserts exactly. If a test of worth is wanted, it lies in the way they ended their lives. This holds not only where that ending set the final seal on a man’s merit, but also where it gave the first sign that he had any. For it is just to claim that steadfastness in his country’s battles should cover a man’s other imperfections like a cloak: the good action has blotted out the bad, and his merit as a citizen has more than outweighed his faults as an individual. Yet none of these men let wealth, with its prospect of future enjoyment, unnerve his spirit, or let poverty, with its hope of a day of freedom and riches, tempt him to shrink from danger. No: they held vengeance upon their enemies to be more desirable than any personal blessing, and reckoned it the most glorious of hazards. So they joyfully chose to accept the risk, to make sure of their vengeance, and to let their wishes wait. They committed to hope the uncertainty of final success, but in the business before them they thought it right to act boldly and trust in themselves. Choosing to die resisting rather than to live submitting, they fled only from dishonor, but met danger face to face; and after one brief moment, at the summit of their fortune, they escaped, not from their fear, but from their glory.

note: Closing quotation mark added; source leaves this speech paragraph unclosed.
replacement: “So died these men, as became Athenians. You, their survivors, must resolve to have as unfaltering a spirit in the field, though you may pray for a happier outcome. Do not be content with ideas drawn only from words about the advantages of defending your country. A speaker could make a valuable text of these even before an audience as alive to them as this one. You must yourselves realize the power of Athens and feed your eyes upon her from day to day, until love of her fills your hearts. Then, when all her greatness has broken upon you, reflect that men won it by courage, a sense of duty, and a keen feeling of honor in action. Reflect too that when they failed in some enterprise, they would not consent to deprive their country of their valor, but laid it at her feet as the most glorious contribution they could offer. All of them gave their lives in common, and each of them received individually that renown which never grows old. They received also a sepulchre: not so much the one where their bones lie, as that noblest of shrines in which their glory is stored up, to be remembered forever whenever deed or story calls for its commemoration. For heroes have the whole earth for their tomb. In lands far from their own, where the column with its epitaph declares it, there is enshrined in every breast an unwritten record, with no tablet to preserve it except that of the heart. Take these men as your model. Judge happiness to be the fruit of freedom, and freedom of valor, and never decline the dangers of war. For it is not the wretched, who have nothing to hope for, who would most justly be unsparing of their lives. It is rather those to whom continued life may bring reverses as yet unknown, and for whom a fall, if it came, would have the most tremendous consequences. And surely, to a man of spirit, the degradation of cowardice is immeasurably more grievous than the unfelt death that strikes him in the midst of his strength and patriotism!

note: Closing quotation mark added; source leaves this speech paragraph unclosed.
replacement: “Comfort, therefore, not condolence, is what I have to offer to those parents of the dead who are here. They know that life is subject to numberless chances; but fortunate are those who draw as their lot a death as glorious as the one that has caused your mourning, and whose lives have been measured so exactly that they end in the happiness in which they were spent. Still, I know this is a hard saying, especially since you will constantly be reminded of the dead when you see in other people’s homes the blessings in which you once took pride. For grief is felt not so much for the want of what we have never known as for the loss of what we have long been used to. Yet you who are still of an age to have children must bear up in the hope of having others in their place. They will help you to forget those you have lost, and they will be to the state both a reinforcement and a security; for no fair or just policy can be expected from a citizen who does not, like his fellows, bring a father’s interests and apprehensions to the decision. As for those of you who are past your prime, you must count it a gain that the best part of your life was fortunate, and that the short span that remains will be cheered by the fame of the departed. For only the love of honor never grows old; and what rejoices the heart of age and helplessness is honor, not gain, as some would have it.

note: Closing quotation mark added; source leaves this speech paragraph unclosed.
replacement: “To the sons or brothers of the dead I turn next, and I see a hard struggle before you. When a man is gone, everyone is accustomed to praise him. However transcendent your merit, you will find it difficult not only to overtake their renown but even to come near it. The living have envy to contend with, while those who are no longer in our path are honored with a goodwill that rivalry does not touch. And if I must say something on the subject of female excellence to those of you who will now be widows, one short exhortation will contain it all. Great will be your glory if you do not fall short of your natural character, and greatest will be the glory of the woman who is least talked of among the men, whether for good or for bad.

note: Closing quotation mark added; source leaves this speech paragraph unclosed.
replacement: “My task is now finished. I have performed it as well as I could, and as far as words go, the requirements of the law are satisfied. As for deeds, those who lie buried here have already received part of their honors, and the rest they will receive through their children, who will be brought up at public expense until they are grown. In this way the state offers a valuable prize, like the garland of victory in this race of valor, both to those who have fallen and to their survivors. And where the rewards for merit are greatest, there the best citizens are found.
